title: Trapped in a Bad Cleaning Contract? Here's Why We'll Never Make You Sign One
meta_description: Most San Antonio cleaning companies lock owners into contracts with penalty clauses. Chabod uses a scope of work instead — here's the difference, and why it protects you better.
content_html:
We don't make clients sign a cleaning contract because a standard contract's termination-penalty clause exists to guarantee the company gets paid regardless of quality — not to guarantee quality itself. Instead, we ask every client to sign a scope of work: a written record of exactly what's included and excluded, with no termination clause, no notice period, and no penalty for leaving once service has started.

Here's a scenario a lot of San Antonio hosts have lived through: you sign with a cleaning company, everything's fine for a month, and then it isn't. Cleaners start showing up late. Details get missed. You raise it, nothing changes. You look at your contract to see how to get out — and there it is. A ninety-day notice period. An early termination fee. A clause that basically says: you're stuck, or you're stuck and it costs you to leave.

That's not a rare horror story. That's just how most service contracts in this industry are built. And once you understand why, you'll understand why we do things differently.

What a contract actually is

Strip away the legal language, and a standard cleaning contract is really just this: you agree to pay on a schedule, we agree to show up on a schedule, and if either side wants out before the term ends, there's a penalty for leaving early or without enough notice.

That penalty is the entire point of the contract. It's not there to guarantee quality — it's there to guarantee payment, regardless of quality. If a company is confident they'll keep earning your business every single time, they don't need a penalty clause to keep you. The fact that so many companies use one tells you something about how confident they actually are in their own consistency.

What we ask you to sign instead: a scope of work

We don't use service contracts with termination clauses. What we do ask every owner to sign, after we talk through your property, is a scope of work.

A scope of work is not a commitment to stay with us for six months. It's a written record of exactly what's included in your cleaning fee — and just as importantly, what isn't. Which rooms, which tasks, whether we're adjusting pool chemicals, whether we're handling carpet or upholstery cleaning, whatever applies to your specific property.

Why bother writing that down if there's no penalty attached to it? Because six months from now, neither of us should have to rely on memory. If we agreed in early 2026 that pool chemical adjustment wasn't part of the standard turnover fee, that document settles the question the moment it comes up again — no argument, no "I thought that was included," no awkward conversation. It protects you as much as it protects us.

The scope of work is where your SOP starts

Here's the part that makes this more than paperwork: the scope of work isn't just a boundary line, it's the starting point for the actual system your cleaners follow.

We don't build a standard operating procedure for carpet cleaning or pool chemical checks speculatively, on the chance a client might want it someday. We build it the moment it's agreed to in your scope of work — and not before. What's included or excluded is never decided by guessing what a cleaner should or shouldn't do. It's decided by one question first: did we actually talk about this and agree to it?

That order matters. Once carpet cleaning is agreed to for your property, that's what triggers us to bring the right equipment, train your assigned cleaner on that specific machine, and document the exact procedure so it isn't dependent on one person's memory. The same cleaner — or a different one three months from now — follows the same steps and gets the same result. That's the whole point of an SOP: not creativity, repeatability.

So the scope of work and the SOP aren't two separate things. One leads directly into the other. The scope tells us what you're paying for. The SOP is how we guarantee it looks the same way every single time, whether it's turnover forty or turnover four hundred.

What's missing from our scope of work, on purpose

No termination clause. No notice period. No penalty for leaving once service has started. No auto-renewal buried in fine print. If you want to stop using Chabod tomorrow, you stop using Chabod tomorrow. (The one thing new clients put down is a $50 booking deposit to hold the date. It is credited toward the first visit, and we refund it in full if we are the ones who cancel.) You're not paying us for paperwork that keeps you here — you're paying us, turnover by turnover, for a job actually done right.

So what actually keeps you with us?

Honestly — the same thing that should keep any cleaning company accountable: doing the job well enough, consistently enough, that leaving never crosses your mind. That's backed by real process on our end, not a signature on your end. It starts with the scope of work you agreed to, runs through the specific SOP built for your property, and ends with checklist-based turnovers, photo documentation on every job, and a quality-control review before anything is marked complete.

We'd rather earn your business every time your calendar shows a checkout than rely on a clause that makes leaving expensive. If we start missing details, you should be free to walk — and you are.

The tradeoff, stated plainly

This isn't the cheapest way to run a cleaning business, and we're not going to pretend otherwise. Consistency costs something to maintain. What you're paying for is peace of mind that doesn't depend on legal language to enforce it — just a documented scope of work, a property-specific SOP built from it, and a track record that speaks for itself turnover after turnover.
